On Ramchandra Ray's escape night, Udayaditya confronts Sitaram with a sword and binds/disarms him to leave; on Udayaditya's prison escape night, Sitaram opens the cell, grabs and carries him out amid fire and leads him away, reversing who restrains whom.

Pratapaditya's initial plan was to have two Pathan men kill Basanta Ray when Basanta Ray took shelter at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore; this failed when one of the Pathans refused and revealed the plot. Basanta Ray is finally ended by a sword: after Muktiyar Khan presents Pratapaditya's signed death order, Abdul strikes him with a drawn sword.

The covert poisoning—secretly procured from Mangala (Rukmini) via Matangini and consumed by Surma—causes her death/departure.
Ramchandra Ray decides to take another wife, so when Vibha finally reaches Chandradwip he is already marrying another woman.

Rukmini obtains Udayaditya’s ring, whose seal bears his name, and it is used to stamp a forged treason petition against him; Bhagavat presents this petition to Pratapaditya, who then has Udayaditya imprisoned.

Ramchandra’s escape forces Udayaditya to coerce guards such as Sitaram, leading to their dismissal; Udayaditya and then Surma secretly continue paying them stipends after Pratapaditya forbids it, and when this secret aid is discovered, Pratapaditya orders Surma sent to her paternal home.

It expresses Basanta Ray’s lonely grief and longing for loved ones who are absent/gone, sung without joy; he first sings/hums it alone at sunset on the Raigarh veranda, and later sings it slowly while holding Vibha’s hand in Surma’s empty room in Jessore.

After failing to stop the escape, Rukmini survived and told Pratapaditya that Udayaditya had fled with Basanta Ray and that Sitaram had set the fire; Pratapaditya then sent Muktiyar Khan with a secret order to execute the King of Raigarh, and Rukmini guided soldiers to capture Udayaditya at Raigarh, after which Muktiyar Khan carried out Basanta Ray’s death sentence.

Pratapaditya initially receives Ramchandra coldly and dismissively, treating him as socially inferior (minimal welcome, little attention, and sending him to the inner quarters), while later in Ramchandra’s own court Pratapaditya’s status is repeatedly mocked and belittled by courtiers, with Ramchandra enjoying and participating in the ridicule.

She leaves Raigarh, renames herself Mangala, and lives on the outskirts of Jessore; from there she monitors the palace, prepares poison (fetched via Matangini for the Rajmahishi) associated with Surma’s death, and later enters Udayaditya’s chamber during a storm to manipulate him and take his ring.

His early lament that he was unfit and unhappy as crown prince culminates when, brought before Pratapaditya, he declares himself unworthy of the kingdom, refuses it, asks for release, and formally swears before Ma-Kali never to accept or rule any part of Jessore's kingdom, naming Samaraditya the heir.

It is intercepted when Nayanchand, afraid of what Pratapaditya might do, gives the letter to the Mahisi instead of delivering it as intended; the Mahisi then, following Basanta Ray’s advice, misrepresents its contents to Vibha by announcing that Ramchandra Ray wrote requesting that Vibha be sent to her in-laws’ house, hiding that he had spitefully renounced her.

Pratapaditya had the canal adjoining the palace blocked with large sal-wood logs to trap Ramchandra Ray's boat, but during the escape Rammohan and his followers pulled the boat up and over the logs, while the guards' pursuit boat arrived far too late due to delays, so the trap failed.

Basanta Ray leaves his beloved sitar behind and can no longer play it through his tears, later saying its strings are broken and it cannot be tuned, mirroring his deepening despair as Udayaditya is separated from him and eventually imprisoned.

He changes from fearlessly intervening to protect subjects and resist oppression, regardless of consequences, to a state of paralyzing fear and hesitation after Surma's death, in which he withdraws from helping or intervening even when witnessing oppression.
He rescues Udayaditya from prison during the fire, opening his cell and leading him out.

In one instance he carries Ramchandra Ray on his back down a rope from the palace roof and lowers him into a boat; in the other he lifts unconscious Vibha, carries her out of the palace, and places her in a palanquin/boat.

In Jessore, she is heavily and royally adorned by the Mahishi—gold bangles, diamond bracelet, large nose ring, styled hair—while in Chandradwip she dresses as a common woman/beggar-like, veiled, and enters the palace like a maidservant without welcome.

In his bedchamber after Surma’s death, the window is tied to Surma’s absent seat and his lingering hope of seeing her there; in the prison cell, it becomes a small opening onto sky, birds, and hope of future freedom, while the bed/cot becomes the real prison.

Sitaram initially borrows money from Rukmini with playful, flirtatious banter and never repays, later secretly conferring with her; after Udayaditya’s imprisonment, he angrily blames and threatens her while she claims the Yubaraj as hers; later, during the escape plan and fire, he stops at her house assuming she is dead to steal her money, finds her alive and threatening, and she seizes a curved blade to attack him, forcing him to flee.

The guardhouse fire begins as a diversion that draws guards away from Udayaditya’s prison, but Sitaram then escalates it: his men help prolong the blaze, set Udayaditya’s empty cell on fire, add bones, a skull, and his sword, and spread the claim that he died in the fire, thereby turning a distraction into a cover-up of his escape.
He is ungrateful: he assumes Udayaditya saved him for his sister’s sake rather than out of concern for him, and in court he joins in mocking Udayaditya as merely Pratapaditya’s son.

The Emperor-of-Delhi threat is first raised by the minister and dismissed by Pratapaditya; later, Bhagavat and Sitaram forge a petition purporting that Udayaditya is complaining to the Emperor about Pratapaditya’s treason, and Bhagavat presents it to Pratapaditya as an intercepted document, turning the abstract imperial threat into apparent evidence against his son.

In Chapter 8, Vibha secretly has Surma style her hair to her own liking, showing Surma's presence and intimacy in the palace; later, after Surma's disappearance, Vibha sits quietly at braiding time as if Surma will come to braid it, but her hair remains unbraided/unkempt, making the undone hairstyle a visible sign of Surma's tragic absence.
